system: You are an AI assistant whose primary goal is to organise the limitations of a scientific paper so that researchers can turn them into well-scoped follow-up research problems. You are precise, you do not invent limitations, and you only use the information given.
user:
The base paper is:
Title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD

A previous critical-appraisal step (a multi-agent limitation-extraction pipeline) produced the following 39
limitations of the base paper. Each line gives the id, the importance assigned by that step (1-5), the aspect, and
the limitation with its explanation:

L1 [importance 5, Experimental Design]. All few-shot results come from a single random K-shot draw with no repeated runs, error bars, confidence intervals or statistical tests, and performance is non-monotonic in K (HIS AC 85.10 at K=8 falls to 82.62 at K=16; LiverCT 85.90 falls to 83.85). With K as small as 2, the choice of support images dominates the outcome, so marginal differences (e.g., 99.38 vs 99.41 AUC) cannot be distinguished from sampling noise; the non-monotonic shot trend suggests instability or overfitting to the tiny support set. Consequently the abstract's 'significantly surpasses' wording, the K=4 headline table, the ensemble/dual-adapter ablations and the shot-count figures are not statistically supported.
L2 [importance 5, Experimental Design]. No patient-, volume- or slide-level split verification is reported for BrainMRI, LiverCT, OCT17, ChestXray or HIS, so correlated 2D slices/patches from the same case may straddle the train/test boundary. BrainMRI slices are cut from BraTS FLAIR volumes, LiverCT slices from BTCV/LiTS scans and HIS patches from 115 Camelyon16 WSIs; if slices or patches of the same volume/slide appear in both sets, the reported AUCs measure memorization rather than generalization, and slice/patch-level AUC is presented as if observations were independent (HIS: 1,003 normal + 997 abnormal patches from only 115 WSIs). Leakage therefore cannot be ruled out for the headline numbers.
L3 [importance 5, Experimental Design]. The 'zero-shot' protocol is not supervision-free: adapters are trained on labeled medical images (and dense masks) from the five remaining datasets, with per-fold source budgets unreported, and the resulting model is compared against a training-free baseline (WinCLIP). 'Zero-shot' here means only that the target modality/anatomy is unseen; the source pool includes thousands of normal images plus labeled subsets (83-1,490 labeled images per dataset) and the leave-one-out folds differ greatly in size, so the reported 20.34-point AC gain over WinCLIP compares a heavily supervised model with an unsupervised one and the 'lightweight' framing is unsupported. The zero-shot numbers therefore do not establish transfer without medical labels.
L4 [importance 5, Experimental Design]. The few-shot protocol is under-specified: the paper never states the normal/anomalous composition of the K labeled samples, whether K counts total images or images per class, how subsets are seeded, or whether the K target samples are used alone or together with labeled data from the other five datasets. The appendix only says a 'random subset of labeled training samples' is drawn from a pool containing both normal and anomalous images. If a K=2 draw contains no anomaly, the claimed benefit of abnormal supervision disappears; if cross-dataset labeled data is also used, MVFA is not a pure few-shot target-domain learner and the comparison with baselines trained on K target samples is unfair. The protocol therefore cannot be replicated or interpreted, and the shot-count trends are uninterpretable.
L5 [importance 4, Methodology]. The multi-level alignment loss applies Dice and Focal losses against pixel masks at every level to all datasets, yet OCT17, ChestXray and HIS provide only image-level labels and the treatment of the missing masks is never specified. The loss definition requires a ground-truth mask S for every training tuple, so for the three image-label-only datasets the segmentation terms are either ill-defined, silently dropped, or replaced by undocumented pseudo-masks. This makes the numbers on half the benchmark non-reproducible, means the effective objective differs across folds, and means the segmentation branch is validated on only BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC — so the claim of one universal AC+AS model is unsupported for image-label-only data.
L6 [importance 4, Methodology]. The few-shot branch's memory bank is built exclusively from labeled normal images, so the labeled abnormal samples never serve as test-time references and the branch remains a one-class nearest-neighbour detector. The paper credits its advantage over CLIP/WinCLIP to 'utilizing a few abnormal samples', yet those anomalies influence only the adapter training loss; the test-time score is still the minimum cosine distance to normal references (at K=2 the normality model consists of only two feature sets), inheriting the ambiguous-boundary weakness the paper attributes to normal-only AD methods. This also conflicts with the Introduction's statement that testing uses 'additional referenced image features if available', leaving the inference mechanism internally inconsistent.
L7 [importance 4, Results & Analysis]. Headline averages mask per-dataset regressions and unequal evaluation subsets: AC averages use six datasets while AS averages use only the three mask datasets, the +7.33 AC gain over APRIL-GAN is dominated by LiverCT where APRIL-GAN is near chance (~3.2 points excluding it), and MVFA is worse than APRIL-GAN on BrainMRI zero-shot AS (90.27 vs 91.79) and than DRA/APRIL-GAN on OCT17 at K=2. Averaging over datasets lets a single baseline failure inflate the headline, and the abstract presents the AC and AS averages side by side without qualification, so a reader cannot tell that the segmentation evidence covers only BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC or that the method loses on several dataset/shot combinations. The 'significantly surpasses' framing is therefore not supported uniformly, and the near-saturated AS metric (97-99%) leaves little headroom to demonstrate the multi-level AS design.
L8 [importance 4, Results & Analysis]. Evaluation is limited to ROC AUC: no Dice/IoU, PRO/AUPRO, boundary metrics, lesion-level sensitivity, PR-AUC, sensitivity/specificity at a clinically chosen threshold, or calibration are reported. Pixel-level AUC pools all pixels and is dominated by abundant background, so a model that over-segments can still score 97-99% and the small AS gains cannot be interpreted as better localization; the near-ceiling values also leave almost no dynamic range for comparing methods. For classification, AUC says nothing about the operating point or whether the probability-like scores are calibrated, so the clinical usability of the outputs is unassessed.
L9 [importance 4, Methodology]. Prompt construction is ambiguous and unaudited: the main text describes generic normal/anomalous states while the appendix substitutes target organ names, the 35 templates are averaged into a single 2×d feature with no selection criterion or validation protocol, and no prompt ablation is reported. If per-organ prompts are used, the zero-shot protocol requires knowing the target anatomy at inference — privileged target metadata that weakens the 'unseen anatomical region' claim — while if only generic prompts are used the appendix description is misleading. The template-selection procedure is undocumented (raising the possibility of test-set contamination), and the fixed generic wording cannot express lesion-type-specific semantics, so the contribution of the text branch and the reproducibility of the headline comparisons are unknown.
L10 [importance 4, Methodology]. The test-time fusion is under-specified: the paper never states whether the few-shot memory-bank branch is active in the zero-shot folds (where no target-domain references exist), never reports zero-only/few-only/fused scores separately, and sums a softmax probability with a cosine distance at fixed 0.5/0.5 weights without scale calibration. The final prediction is defined as a fixed 0.5/0.5 mixture of the two branches, but the few-shot branch requires labeled images from the same modality/anatomy as the test sample, which contradicts the zero-shot definition; if it is disabled the published formula does not apply to the zero-shot tables, and if it is populated with source normals the 'zero-shot' label is misleading. Because the two branches live on different scales and no branch-wise ablation is given, the contribution of each component to the headline numbers cannot be assessed and the zero-shot results cannot be reproduced from the text.
L11 [importance 4, Experimental Design]. Zero-shot generalization is assessed with exactly one leave-one-dataset-out fold per target on a single benchmark, so sensitivity to the choice of held-out modality combination is unknown, and cross-modality generalization is confounded with cross-dataset/artifact recognition. With one source combination per target, the headline averages depend entirely on which five datasets form the training pool (whose sizes differ by orders of magnitude) and no alternative source mixes are reported. Because each target differs from its sources in acquisition pipeline, scanner, population and annotation protocol simultaneously, a model could succeed by recognizing dataset-specific artifacts rather than modality-invariant anomaly cues; the LiverCT benchmark itself shows such cross-dataset splits are feasible but they are not used to isolate modality shift.
L12 [importance 4, Experimental Design]. Baseline supervision budgets are unequal and largely undocumented: the few-shot table mixes full-normal-shot, few-normal-shot and few-shot methods trained on very different amounts of data, per-fold source data/annotation access for APRIL-GAN and WinCLIP is unspecified, and MedCLIP's stronger ChestXray score is attributed by the authors to training on overlapping ChestXray data. PatchCore, CFlowAD, RD4AD and MKD are trained on thousands of normal images while MVFA uses K labeled images, and the paper acknowledges the asymmetry yet still frames the comparison as evidence of superiority; if baselines received fewer annotations or different source subsets than MVFA, the gains reflect unequal supervision rather than architecture. The ChestXray column is additionally not an out-of-domain test for MedCLIP, so the 'unseen modality' framing does not hold for every baseline in the table.
L13 [importance 4, Experimental Design]. Binary anomaly labels are semantically heterogeneous and their construction is undocumented: ChestXray's positive class mixes 'Lung Opacity' with 'No Lung Opacity/Not Normal' cases from a pneumonia-detection challenge, and OCT17's three anomaly types are collapsed into one positive class, with only aggregate AUCs reported. A positive class that mixes opacity with 'not normal but no opacity' may let the model learn non-opacity findings or dataset artifacts, and collapsing three OCT anomaly types hides which pathologies are detected and can inflate AUC if some types dominate. Without per-anomaly-type results it is unknown whether one model handles diverse anomaly semantics or only dataset-level labels, weakening the 'universal' framing.
L14 [importance 4, Methodology]. The adapter-vs-projector ablation does not isolate the contribution of multi-level placement: the two designs differ structurally and in capacity (no parameter counts are reported), and no matched-budget parameter-efficient baselines (LoRA, prefix/VPT tuning, full fine-tuning) are compared. The paper asserts that 'all other factors, including model parameters, remain constant', but adapters are inserted residually inside the backbone and alter intermediate activations whereas projectors are independent terminal maps, so the gains could stem from added capacity or from the residual path rather than from multi-level adaptation. The related work also omits the PEFT and prompt-ensembling literature that provides the closest precedents, so the novelty and causal attribution of the core contribution are both unestablished.
L15 [importance 4, Methodology]. The 'lightweight' claim is never quantified: no trainable-parameter count, adapter bottleneck width, FLOPs, wall-clock training time, per-image inference latency, peak memory or memory-bank size is reported for MVFA or the baselines. Lightweightness is the central selling point for scarce-data medical use, yet the only compute information given is a single RTX 3090 for 50 epochs. The framework adds three dual bottleneck adapters plus two projectors to a ViT-L/14 backbone, stores four levels of grid features per reference image and adds a nearest-neighbour search whose cost grows with the number of references, so neither the efficiency advantage over full fine-tuning or memory-bank methods nor deployment feasibility on clinical hardware can be judged.
L16 [importance 4, Methodology]. Anomaly maps are produced on the ViT-L/14 patch grid (~16-17 tokens per side at 240 px, each token covering ~14×14 pixels) and bilinearly upsampled, so localization precision is structurally capped and small lesions and boundaries are blurred. Each token covers roughly 14×14 input pixels, so sub-token lesions are unrecoverable and bilinear upsampling inherently blurs boundaries; pixel-level AUC at full resolution therefore reflects coarse patch-level decisions rather than boundary accuracy. No higher-resolution or sliding-window inference variant is evaluated, so the AS numbers cannot be interpreted as lesion-level localization performance.
L17 [importance 4, Clinical & Deployment]. Despite criticizing prior work for requiring per-task retraining, MVFA trains a separate adapter set for every target dataset (50 epochs per fold), and no incremental or continual adaptation procedure is provided. The paper's own formulation includes target-domain labeled data in the adaptation set, so each new modality/anatomy needs its own optimization run; no procedure is given for updating an already-adapted model to a new modality without retraining, and no adaptation time or aggregate compute across the five leave-one-out folds is reported. The 'universal model' and 'flexible adaptation' claims therefore rest on per-target retraining whose cost is unknown, which matters where per-site retraining is impractical.
L18 [importance 4, Clinical & Deployment]. The few-shot protocol still requires expert pixel-level lesion masks for BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC (83, 166 and 115 labeled images annotated with segmentation masks), and the annotation cost, the number of masks needed, and performance without masks are never quantified. The problem formulation makes a full pixel mask part of every training tuple, so 'K=4' means four expertly delineated slices rather than four cheap labels — the most expensive annotation type in medical imaging. Since real deployments typically have only a handful of image-level labels, the practical advantage over normal-only training is overstated in settings where dense masks are expensive, and the paper's scarce-data motivation is not addressed.
L19 [importance 4, Methodology]. The preprocessing and training recipe is largely undocumented: only the 240-pixel input, optimizer, learning rate, batch size and epoch count are given, with no per-modality intensity or stain normalization, resize/crop policy, augmentation, weight decay, scheduler or random seeds. The benchmark spans MRI, CT, OCT, X-ray and histology, where intensity handling (e.g., the abdominal HU window used for LiverCT) and stain appearance strongly affect learned features, and HIS patches are merely described as 'randomly extracted'. Without normalization and augmentation specifications the reported cross-modality gains cannot be separated from preprocessing choices and the results are not independently reproducible.
L20 [importance 4, Experimental Design]. No validation split, early-stopping rule or model-selection criterion is described, so a fixed 50-epoch schedule at constant learning rate 1e-3 is applied blindly to as few as two labeled images, with no convergence, learning-curve or epoch-sensitivity analysis. With K=2, 50 epochs at lr 1e-3 can easily overfit the adapters, and without held-out validation it is impossible to tell whether the reported numbers reflect a converged model or an arbitrary stopping point; the fixed defaults of γ, λ and β also cannot be justified without validation data. This weakens the reliability and reproducibility of the few-shot conclusions, especially at the smallest shot counts.
L21 [importance 4, Clinical & Deployment]. The 'universal' claim is unsupported beyond the six specific public datasets: each modality comes from a single source cohort, no demographic, site, scanner or subgroup analysis is reported, no ethics/data-governance statement is given, and robustness to acquisition shift (scanner, vendor, protocol, field of view) is never evaluated separately from dataset identity. Generalization across modalities is confounded with generalization across institutions and patient populations, since each modality contributes one acquisition pipeline and one cohort (RSNA, BraTS, Camelyon16). Without age/sex/site breakdowns, performance on underrepresented groups and under shifted acquisition conditions is unknown, and the zero-shot protocol changes acquisition pipeline, population and annotation protocol simultaneously so acquisition-shift robustness cannot be isolated.
L22 [importance 4, Experimental Design]. The leave-one-out 'unseen modality and anatomical region' claim does not hold for the OCT17 target, because the training pool then contains RESC, which is also retinal OCT imagery. The protocol is described as training on 'the remaining datasets with different modalities and anatomical regions', yet RESC and OCT17 are both retinal OCT datasets, so the model has already seen retinal (and retinal-edema) appearance when OCT17 is held out. This weakens the central generalization claim and inflates the zero-shot average for that target, and the redundancy persists in later work reusing the same BMAD pool unless the protocol is redefined.
L23 [importance 3, Methodology]. Key design constants (residual ratio γ=0.1, loss weights λ1=λ2=λ3=1.0, branch weights β1=β2=0.5, two-layer adapters, 35-template averaging) are fixed defaults with no sensitivity analysis or validation-based selection. γ controls how much pre-trained knowledge is preserved, λ balances classification against segmentation supervision, and β controls how much the text branch contributes, yet none is swept; with K as small as 2 and no validation split, arbitrary defaults can dominate the reported AUCs. The paper's ablations vary architecture but not these hyperparameters, so the gains cannot be causally attributed to the multi-level design.
L24 [importance 3, Methodology]. Although the backbone weights are frozen, adapter outputs are injected into subsequent encoder blocks, and the residual path's role is never isolated (no γ=0 vs γ=0.1 ablation) nor the retained pre-trained knowledge quantified. Freezing weights does not leave the backbone computation unchanged, because adapted features alter the inputs of later blocks as the paper's own discussion states. Without measuring feature drift or varying the residual ratio, the claim that pre-trained CLIP knowledge is preserved cannot be verified, and the projector ablation's dramatic OCT17 gap (49.85 vs 95.40 AC) suggests the identity/residual path may account for much of the reported gain rather than the learned adapters.
L25 [importance 3, Results & Analysis]. The claim that multi-level training consistently outperforms single-layer training is contradicted by the paper's own ChestXray results (Layer 3: 79.75 without vs 58.32 with; Layer 4: 72.84 vs 64.58). The supplementary tables show ChestXray AC dropping sharply when multi-level training is used, directly contradicting the stated consistency across all layers and suggesting dataset-specific instability of the jointly optimized adapters. The claim should be restated per dataset and the ChestXray failure analyzed.
L26 [importance 3, Experimental Design]. The MVTec 'in-domain' evaluation is not interpretable: the training protocol (K=4 labeled MVTec images vs transfer of medical adapters) is unspecified, the table includes an undescribed 'RegAD' baseline, method naming is inconsistent ('MFA' vs 'MVFA'), MVFA loses to WinCLIP on cable and transistor, and the appendix's 'significantly outperforms' contradicts the main text's 'comparable'. The two possible protocols imply very different claims (in-domain few-shot learning vs medical-to-industrial transfer), yet the paper leaves the protocol unspecified, so the MVTec numbers cannot be interpreted or reproduced. The reported margins (96.2/96.3 vs WinCLIP 95.2/96.3) do not support the supplementary statement that MVFA 'significantly outperforms' competing methods, and calling an industrial benchmark 'in-domain' for a medically adapted model obscures what the table measures.
L27 [importance 3, Results & Analysis]. The architectural ablations yield margins that are not distinguishable from the noise of a single-draw K-shot protocol: the multi-level ensemble beats the best single layer by only 0.13 AC and 0.05 AS points, the dual-adapter gains are +1.29 AC/+0.36 AS on average and reduce OCT17 AC from 99.87 to 99.38, and the adapter-over-projector AS gains are only 0.21-2.88 points (the large gains are classification-only). Without repeated seeds or significance testing, such margins cannot be separated from sampling variability, so the claimed benefits of multi-level training, multi-level ensembling and the dual-adapter design are stronger than the evidence supports; the paper's own wording that the dual design 'outperforms on almost all datasets' glosses over the OCT17 degradation, and the adapter benefit appears to be mainly a classification effect.
L28 [importance 3, Results & Analysis]. Qualitative evidence is limited to selected heatmaps and a single RESC t-SNE plot, with no systematic failure-case taxonomy (by anomaly type, lesion size, anatomical location or acquisition condition) and no quantitative feature-separability measure. t-SNE is a non-metric visualization sensitive to its settings and computed on one of six datasets, so it cannot establish that adapted features are more discriminative; selected example panels are not a representative sample, and the paper's own figures explicitly mark regions that were missed or erroneously segmented. Without a taxonomy or quantification of failures, the conditions under which MVFA breaks down remain unknown and the recalibration/generalization claims are supported only anecdotally.
L29 [importance 3, Literature]. The novelty and positioning claims are weakly supported: the 'first attempt' statement is hedged, no medical-domain AD method (one-class or reconstruction-based) is benchmarked under the same protocol, MedCLIP is absent from the zero-shot table, and the related work omits medical VLMs/foundation models, medical prompt engineering, text-conditioned medical segmentation, PEFT and prompt-learning methods that are the closest methodological neighbours. The paper argues that medical one-class methods need many normal images and generalize poorly, but no such method is tested under the identical leave-one-out or K-shot protocol, so the argument is never examined; the only medical VLM in the tables is absent from the zero-shot comparison. Because the contribution is framed as the first adaptation of pre-trained VLMs to medical zero-/few-shot AD, the priority claim cannot be verified and the contribution cannot be positioned against the closest competitors.
L30 [importance 3, Methodology]. The anomaly-classification scoring pipeline is ambiguous: the paper never specifies which softmax class is scored, over which axis the maximum is taken, or how the binary label is encoded for the BCE loss. The zero-shot AC score is written as a max over G of a two-class softmax and the BCE target is the symbol c, so different readings (max over spatial positions of the anomalous-class probability vs max over classes) give different scores and calibrations. Because AUC is rank-based this does not by itself invalidate the reported numbers, but it prevents exact reproduction and interpretation of the anomaly scores shown qualitatively.
L31 [importance 3, Experimental Design]. No simple supervised baseline trained on the identical K labeled images (e.g., a linear probe on frozen CLIP features or a compact U-Net/nnU-Net) is provided, so the necessity of the multi-level VLM machinery in the K-shot regime is untested. All competing methods are industrial or general-purpose AD systems, and none is a minimal medical-domain supervised model trained on the same K images and masks. Without such a control, the gains cannot be attributed to multi-level visual-language adaptation rather than to generic fine-tuning on a handful of labeled medical images, and the segmentation comparison lacks a clinically relevant reference point.
L32 [importance 3, Experimental Design]. All results use a single backbone and input resolution (CLIP ViT-L/14 at 240 px), so it is unclear whether the gains come from the multi-level design or from the choice of pre-trained encoder, and portability to other backbones is unknown. Without varying the encoder family, patch size or input resolution, the paper cannot show that multi-level adaptation is the source of the improvement; later work varies both encoder family and resolution and adds spatial priors, indicating that backbone choice materially affects zero-shot AD performance.
L33 [importance 3, Methodology]. Volumetric MRI and CT are reduced to independent 2D slices (BraTS FLAIR slices 60-100; CT axial slices), so the method cannot model through-plane context or patient-level lesion extent. Each 2D PNG slice is scored independently, so anomalies interpretable only in 3D context, or spanning several slices, are handled inconsistently and no volume-level decision is produced. Later benchmarking of CLIP-based zero-shot AD on brain MRI highlights spatial-consistency limitations of 2D approaches for 3D problems.
L34 [importance 3, Results & Analysis]. Near-perfect AUCs (e.g., LiverCT AS 99.73, OCT17 AC 99.38) are reported without any contamination check against CLIP's web-scale pre-training data or validation on an external cohort. CLIP was pre-trained on internet image-text pairs and the benchmarks (RSNA, BraTS, Camelyon16) are public, so evaluation images may overlap with pre-training data; the CLIP authors' own overlap analysis shows such contamination can inflate zero-shot accuracy. The reported gains therefore cannot be read as reflecting clinical difficulty, and later review work explicitly flags MVFA's >99% numbers as potentially reflecting easy datasets or leakage.
L35 [importance 3, Clinical & Deployment]. The paper frames medical AD as 'preventing misdiagnoses and facilitating early interventions', but the outputs are binary normal/anomalous scores and generic-prompt heatmaps with no diagnostic type, severity or calibration, which cannot support those clinical claims. The method produces a generic anomaly score and a coarse anomaly map derived from prompts that only distinguish normal from anomalous, so it cannot indicate what the abnormality is or how urgent it is. Without pathology typing, localization validation against clinical annotations or operating-point analysis, the diagnostic framing is substantially stronger than the evidence; the conclusion's more cautious 'promising research avenues' wording is better aligned with the demonstrated capability.
L36 [importance 3, Methodology]. The zero-shot adaptation may encode source-domain-specific cues rather than transferable abnormality features, and the paper contains no diagnostic test of this. The adapters are trained on five heterogeneous source datasets against a single generic normal/abnormal text target, so nothing prevents the adapted features from keying on source-specific appearance (CT texture, MRI contrast, stain colour) instead of abnormality. Later work explicitly targets this failure mode with domain-adversarial visual learning and source-only feature mixing and reports that source-domain dependency degrades unseen-target performance, so the cross-domain claim rests on an untested assumption.
L37 [importance 3, Experimental Design]. The zero-shot comparison uses only WinCLIP and April-GAN, and the MVFA-AD numbers later papers cite do not match MVFA's own reported zero-shot results, so the state-of-the-art ranking is not protocol-matched. MVFA's own zero-shot BrainMRI result is 78.63/90.27, whereas a later paper's table lists MVFA-AD at 88.9/89.3 for BrainMRI, indicating the two numbers come from different protocols or splits; treating them as identical is invalid. The baseline set also omits learnable-prompt CLIP methods that later work reports as stronger, so the zero-shot ranking cannot be verified.
L38 [importance 2, Methodology]. Image-level classification is computed as the maximum over spatial locations of the minimum distance to the normal memory bank, so a single outlier patch determines the image score, and this pooling choice is never compared with alternatives. The few-shot AC score takes max_G of a per-patch nearest-normal distance, coupling the global classification task to the most anomalous local region; the paper never compares max with mean or top-k aggregation, nor states whether the text branch uses the same pooling, so the contribution of the 'global' classification branch cannot be isolated. On datasets with large normal anatomy or noisy segmentation this can inflate AC independently of true image-level abnormality.
L39 [importance 2, Experimental Design]. The 'in-domain' columns of the zero-shot table are never defined, so it is impossible to tell what training data they correspond to or how they relate to the leave-one-out protocol. The caption promises an 'in-/out-domain evaluation' while the text describes only leave-one-out training on the remaining datasets. If 'in-domain' means the target dataset's own labeled data was used, those numbers are not zero-shot; if it denotes another split, it is unspecified. Either way the numbers cannot be interpreted or reproduced, and they are used rhetorically to support the generalization narrative.
